claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially exist as a high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy.
Rapid quenching from high temperature is a typical route for obtaining or retaining this single-phase BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between a composition-dependent thermodynamic drive for ordering or phase separation and kinetic barriers to diffusion.
Rapid quenching retains metastable BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 below its high-temperature stability regime because atomic diffusion is insufficient.
Annealing Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 at approximately 800–1000 K provides sufficient atomic mobility to incrementally overcome diffusion barriers.
Enhanced diffusion during annealing permits nucleation and growth of ordered or compositionally distinct secondary phases.
Chemically ordered domains or nanoscale precipitates at phase boundaries mediate the transformation from metastable BCC to more stable configurations.
At high temperature, the BCC phase is stabilized by entropy.
Cooling or intermediate-temperature annealing increases the thermodynamic driving force for chemical ordering or phase separation.
Whether the thermodynamically favored transformation occurs is controlled by the rate of atomic diffusion.
Relative to a rapidly quenched baseline, annealed samples will develop new XRD diffraction peaks.
Annealed samples will exhibit chemical inhomogeneities and nanoscale ordered domains or precipitates detectable by TEM or APT.
The amount and size of ordered domains or precipitates will increase with annealing time.
The relevant test regime is below the high-temperature BCC stability range but above the threshold for significant atomic mobility, approximately 800–1000 K.
Below the proposed temperature range diffusion is negligible, whereas above it additional transformations may occur.
The identity and composition of the secondary phases and the critical transformation time or temperature may vary with small changes in alloy composition and processing history.
The relative magnitudes of the thermodynamic driving force and kinetic barriers have not been quantitatively determined.
A rapidly quenched Cr39Co18FeNiAl7 baseline retains a single-phase BCC structure because diffusion is insufficient.
Failure to detect new diffraction peaks, nanoscale precipitates, or chemical ordering after annealing intended to overcome kinetic barriers would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The target composition is consistently given as Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 except in the baseline, which gives Cr39Co18FeNiAl7 and therefore omits the stated Fe18 and Ni18 fractions.
